channel.title: OT/ICS Threat Intel - Marine
channel.description: Curated OT/ICS advisories, incidents and threat intelligence. Editorial by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

item.title: [Critical] The Coast Guard and FBI boarded two US-bound energy tankers after foreign cyber actors compromised their networks
item.category: Top Story
item.description: A joint US Coast Guard and FBI statement confirms two offshore boardings of US-bound tankers in August, after both vessels’ networks were found compromised by foreign cyber actors. Coast Guard Cyber Command confirmed malicious cyber activity aboard the VL Prosperity, a Liberian-flagged supertanker; both agencies report no operational disruption, vessel instability or environmental impact. The second vessel remains officially unnamed. Iranian state media claims of seized navigation, propulsion and cargo controls, and a 30-hour communications loss, remain unverified; Bloomberg reports CISA said the actors did not appear to take control, and no attribution has been made. For marine operators the finding that matters most is frequency: the Coast Guard counts this among 40–50 similar cyber boardings in the past year, meaning shipboard network compromise is now routine. A separate, unverified crew claim of controlled cargo-safety systems on an LNG carrier is covered below. - Joint US Coast Guard and FBI statement quoted by CyberScoop and The Record; Rear Adm. Amy Grable to CBS News and SecurityWeek; vessel detail and the nearly-20-vessel tracking via gCaptain citing Bloomberg; Cybernews (19 Sep, citing Bloomberg) for the CISA comment; SecurityWeek (17 Sep) for the Mehr claims, attribution status and the 40–50 prior boardings; Industrial Cyber (17 Sep) on the OT and IT assessment; TechCrunch (18 Sep) for the “reportedly” framing of Iranian claims; second vessel named as Kohaku in press reports relayed by The Jerusalem Post and TechRadar; Dragos analysis (24 Sep) restates the confirmed facts, adds none, and treats the Iranian control claims as unverified - Boardings 21 and 24 Aug 2026; joint statement and first reporting 16 Sep 2026, wider reporting 17 Sep 2026; claims re-checked against reporting through 25 Sep 2026 — no new official statement

item.title: [High] The crew of Vivit Africa LNG now say attackers controlled safety-valve, tank-pressure and boil-off systems — a claim no authority or supplier has verified
item.category: Incident — Crew claims attackers controlled cargo-safety systems; cause officially undetermined
item.description: Bloomberg reported on 18 September, in a story republished by gCaptain, that the crew of the Vivit Africa LNG lost access to some internal control systems in early September in the Mediterranean. The crew reported a suspected cyberattack to Korean Register, the vessel’s technical and safety adviser, and Korean Register says its investigation is ongoing. The ship is owned by South Korea’s H-Line Shipping, flagged in Liberia and on long-term time charter to Vitol, which confirmed the charter but gave no further comment. It had loaded at Cameron LNG in Louisiana for the Adriatic LNG terminal near Rovigo, Italy. It abandoned that destination and headed west towards Algeciras, Spain; The Next Web later reported it off Tunisia. The Italian Coast Guard described a malfunction in the systems that monitor cargo parameters, said its cause “could not be identified”, and said it intervened solely for navigation safety; Marine Insight reported on 19 September that the Coast Guard had not established a cyberattack as the cause. Kongsberg Maritime supplies equipment aboard, which Bloomberg describes as positioning, navigation and propulsion technology. Kongsberg says it is too early to draw conclusions about the cause or any security implications. There are no indications of who might be responsible. Bloomberg counts this as the third tanker in about a month tied to suspected cyber activity, after the two vessels the Coast Guard and FBI boarded, but nothing published connects the cases. On 21 September Splash247 published the crew’s own account, sent by email and also reported to Korean Register. The crew claim that during the Gibraltar transit attackers temporarily took control of steam-pressure and safety-valve systems, and that in the Adriatic they took control of tank-pressure control, pressure-relief valves and boil-off gas management, which the crew say significantly increases the risk of tank rupture and explosion. Splash247 states it has not independently verified the claims. Set against that: the Italian Coast Guard, through Capt. Roberto D’Arrigo, still describes only a malfunction in the systems used to monitor cargo parameters, requiring company technicians, with a cause that could not be identified; Kongsberg Maritime says it is too early to draw conclusions; Vitol declined to comment; H-Line and Korean Register did not respond. The vessel idled off Italy without discharging at Adriatic LNG and then sailed west toward Algeciras. This edition therefore carries two layers and keeps them apart. Confirmed: the diversion without discharge and a cargo-monitoring malfunction of undetermined cause. Claimed: a cyber cause and control of safety and boil-off systems. If the claim were confirmed by class, flag or the equipment supplier it would be the first documented hands-on manipulation of an LNG carrier’s cargo-safety systems, and it would move this page’s threat level; until then it is scored as an unconfirmed incident. - Crew account published by Splash247 (21 Sep 2026, labelled unverified by the outlet); Bloomberg via gCaptain (18 Sep 2026) with Italian Coast Guard, Korean Register and Kongsberg Maritime statements; Marine Insight and The Next Web - Incident early Sep 2026; first reported 18 Sep 2026; crew claims published 21 Sep 2026; Korean Register investigation ongoing; no official finding as of 24 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] Malaysia’s Port of Tanjung Pelepas has resumed container operations after a cyber incident halted its terminal
item.category: Incident — Container terminal operations, recovered
item.description: The Port of Tanjung Pelepas said on 15 September that container terminal operations had resumed, with system recovery advancing steadily, after a cybersecurity incident hit its terminal operating systems. The incident was detected at 23:34 local time on 9 September; PTP isolated the affected systems and suspended container handling as a precaution, processed gate-ins manually from the evening of 10 September and began a controlled, phased restart the same day. A Maersk spokesperson — the port is a Maersk and MMC joint venture — confirmed the incident to The Loadstar and said some vessels might be delayed; the Maersk Hanoi deviated by about ten hours, while a Kuehne+Nagel summary of Lloyd’s List reporting noted no significant queues. PTP says there is no evidence of unauthorised access to customer data. No attacker or initial access vector has been disclosed, and sources differ on how long handling stopped, from several hours to about a day. One development since is a claim, not a finding. On 11 September the DireWolf ransomware group listed the Port of Tanjung Pelepas on its leak site, and ransomware-tracking aggregators record the listing as claiming about 200 GB of data. The claim has not been verified. PTP has not said the incident was ransomware, and neither PTP, its shareholders nor Malaysia’s NACSA has publicly named an attacker. PTP’s own position remains that it has found no evidence of unauthorised access to customer data. Treat the listing as a reason to prepare for possible data exposure, not as attribution. PTP handled more than 14m TEU in 2025 and anchors the Gemini network of Maersk and Hapag-Lloyd. It remains the clearest recent demonstration that a terminal does not need its cranes touched to stop. - Port of Tanjung Pelepas statements to WorldCargo News and an A.P. Moller-Maersk statement to The Loadstar; Kuehne+Nagel summary of Lloyd’s List reporting; DireWolf leak-site listing as recorded by ransomware.live and RedPacket Security (claim only) - Incident detected 9 Sep 2026; phased restart began 10 Sep 2026; DireWolf listing 11 Sep 2026; operations resumed per PTP 15 Sep 2026; no official statement on the claim as of 24 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] Undocumented cellular modems in ZPMC ship-to-shore cranes — confirmed hardware, assessed intent, no observed use
item.category: Threat Intelligence — Supply chain, ship-to-shore crane control
item.description: This is standing context rather than new reporting: US Maritime Administration Advisory 2026-007 was issued on 24 April 2026 and remains in force to 21 October, and the distinction inside the crane supply-chain problem is the part worth carrying into a risk register. What is confirmed is physical: US Coast Guard and congressional inspections found undocumented cellular modems fitted to cranes built by Shanghai Zhenhua Heavy Industries, wired with direct access to the crane industrial controllers and bypassing the port firewalls that are meant to sit in front of them. What is assessed rather than observed is the consequence — an intelligence judgement that those modems could be used to monitor crane activity or disable cranes during a crisis. No such use has been reported anywhere, and this is structural exposure rather than an incident. The reason it still matters is population. ZPMC builds an estimated 72–78 per cent of the world’s ship-to-shore cranes and roughly 80 per cent of those installed in US and European ports, so the exposure is most of the fleet rather than an unlucky subset. MARAD Advisory 2026-007 names ZPMC cranes alongside China’s LOGINK logistics-data platform and Nuctech scanning systems as foreign adversarial technology risks to US port infrastructure, and asks facilities to apply access control, network segmentation and monitoring and offline backups, and to report anomalies to the Coast Guard, CISA and the FBI. Ports are responding with retrofits — removing the foreign modems, replacing crane software, separating crane OT networks — supported by an executive order and more than $20bn in federal loans, with Konecranes and a revived Mitsui E&S North American line named as alternative suppliers. - US Maritime Administration Advisory 2026-007, which names ZPMC cranes, LOGINK and Nuctech directly; inspection and retrofit details from earlier public reporting - MARAD Advisory 2026-007 issued 24 Apr 2026 and in force through 21 Oct 2026

item.title: [High] ENISA says China-linked Mustang Panda has run continuous espionage campaigns against maritime organisations in at least seven EU member states
item.category: Threat Intelligence — State-linked espionage, EU maritime
item.description: ENISA’s Threat Landscape 2026, as reported by Splash247 on 23 September, names Mustang Panda as running “continuous campaigns against maritime-related organisations across at least seven EU member states.” The methods it describes are spear-phishing, compromised USB drives and a range of malware including customised versions of the PlugX remote-access tool. The report gives transport 8% of cyber events, with water transport 16.4% of transport-sector incidents, and classes both maritime and rail transport as a cyber “risk zone.” The activity is described as cyberespionage and strategic intelligence collection rather than immediate operational disruption. No disruption is reported, and no individual victims are named. Splash247’s piece also cites a 103% rise in recorded maritime cyber incidents in 2025, but that figure comes from SplashTech’s own February reporting, not ENISA, so it is not used here. For operators the useful point is the delivery method. USB drives and phishing are the vectors that reach vessels and terminals through crews, contractors and chart or software updates. Espionage access of this kind is also the foothold that could later be used for more than collection. - ENISA Threat Landscape 2026 as reported by Splash247 (Sam Chambers) and Industrial Cyber; ENISA’s own report text not reviewed directly for this edition - Reported 23 Sep 2026

item.title: [Info] In a Honeywell vendor survey, 87% of maritime respondents report a significant OT cyber incident in the past year. Read it as a self-reported figure, not an incident count
item.category: Threat Intelligence & Research — Vendor survey
item.description: Honeywell published its 2026 OT cybersecurity report on 22 September. It is based on a survey of more than 600 industrial cybersecurity leaders across sectors including energy, oil and gas, healthcare, maritime and manufacturing, in the Americas, EMEA and APAC. According to Honeywell, 87% of maritime respondents reported experiencing a significant OT cybersecurity incident in the past 12 months, second only to energy and utilities at 91%. Across all respondents, only 21% reported a complete inventory of their OT assets. Respondents’ most significant incidents caused an average of 16.2 hours of downtime, with losses reported of up to $500,000 per hour. The caveats matter. This is a vendor survey from a company that sells OT security. The figures are self-reported, the release does not define “significant incident,” and it does not give the number of maritime respondents. The 87% figure is not a count of confirmed incidents and should not be quoted as one. Its practical use is the gap it points to: most respondents cannot list their OT assets, and without that list you cannot tell whether an incident touched OT. - Honeywell press release on its 2026 OT cybersecurity report (vendor survey of 600+ industrial cybersecurity leaders); Industrial Cyber coverage - Published 22 Sep 2026

item.title: [Info] The Port of Los Angeles says it blocked around 120 million attack attempts in August — a volume figure, not an incident, and worth reading as such
item.category: Threat Intelligence & Research — Port statistics, blocked attempts
item.description: Port of Los Angeles Executive Director Gene Seroka told Bloomberg Television, in an interview reported by gCaptain on 17 September, that the port blocked more than 120 million intrusion, network-exploitation, credential-harvesting and malware attempts in August 2026. He described a seven-layer cyber operations arrangement run with private-sector partners and put the asymmetry plainly: the attackers only have to get it right once. No successful intrusion and no operational impact was reported. Two cautions apply. The figure counts attempts blocked by automated controls, which at internet-facing scale is dominated by commodity scanning and credential stuffing, so it says more about the port’s exposure and telemetry than about targeting. And it is a public statement, not an audited metric. Its use for other ports is comparative: if your own perimeter reports a number two orders of magnitude smaller, the likelier explanation is that you are not counting rather than that you are not being probed. - Gene Seroka, Port of Los Angeles, on Bloomberg Television — reported by gCaptain - Statement reported 17 Sep 2026; figure covers August 2026

item.title: [Medium] August set a global ransomware record at 997 attacks, with utilities among the categories driving the rise
item.category: Threat Intelligence & Research — Sector statistics
item.description: Comparitech data reported on 14 September recorded 997 ransomware attacks worldwide in August 2026 — an average of 32 a day, a 23 percent increase on July’s 809, and above the previous monthly record of 988. The reporting singles out utility, healthcare and business-services attacks as the categories behind the surge. Treat the absolute number with the usual caution — counts of this kind depend on leak-site claims and disclosure practice as much as on actual incident volume, and claimed victims are not confirmed victims. The direction of travel, however, is consistent with what operators are seeing. Port, terminal and logistics operators sit inside the business-services and transport categories driving this record. For maritime the relevant point is that a terminal does not need its cranes encrypted to stop — losing the terminal operating system, gate systems or EDI is enough. - Comparitech monthly ransomware tracking — reporting via Industrial Cyber - Data for August 2026; reporting published 14 Sep 2026

item.title: [Info] Cyber-informed engineering argues the useful question is not how to keep attackers out, but which consequences you can design away
item.category: Threat Intelligence & Research — Analysis, engineering practice
item.description: An analysis published 15 September sets out the case for cyber-informed engineering in critical infrastructure: that industrial systems operate under a constraint IT does not share, because a compromised network does not automatically have to become a catastrophic physical event. The argument is to move the security question upstream into design — identifying the physical consequences that actually matter, then engineering them out with controls that do not depend on the digital system remaining trustworthy. For ships and terminals the argument lands naturally, because the sector already thinks in terms of consequence and redundancy. The question it asks is whether the engineered fallbacks — manual steering, local crane control, mechanical stops — are genuinely independent of the digital systems they are meant to back up. This is practitioner analysis rather than incident reporting; it names no victim and describes no attack, but it is the most useful lens available for operators whose detection budget will never match their consequence exposure. - Industrial Cyber feature analysis on cyber-informed engineering - Published 15 Sep 2026

item.title: [Info] The monitoring problem nobody wants to say out loud: you cannot scan a running engine room
item.category: Threat Intelligence & Research — Analysis, monitoring practice
item.description: An analysis published by Cybersecurity Insiders on 12 September sets out the visibility gap in shipboard OT in plainer terms than most vendor material manages. Propulsion, steering, ballast, power-management, cargo and navigation systems are increasingly networked, while much of the equipment is ageing, vendor-specific and connected intermittently over satellite. The argument the piece makes is one many fleet security teams have reached independently: active interrogation — the scanning and polling that works on a corporate network — is not safe against safety-critical control systems at sea, so passive, non-intrusive monitoring with local collection and shore-based analysis is the realistic path to continuous anomaly detection. It also flags the exposure growing fastest: remote maintenance, satellite links, autonomous shipping, electrification and automated ports. Treat this as informed practitioner analysis rather than incident reporting — it describes no attack and names no victim — but it maps directly onto what IMO and IACS now expect operators to be able to demonstrate. - Cybersecurity Insiders analysis — surfaced via the Viakoo daily OT briefing. Practitioner analysis, not incident reporting; no primary-source incident underlies it - Published 12 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] Zyxel GS1900 switches enter KEV after GreyNoise documents 996 compromised units — the small managed switch a contractor leaves in the gatehouse
item.category: Critical Advisory — Actively exploited, CISA KEV, small-site switches
item.description: CISA added CVE-2026-7273 to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 21 September with a federal remediation deadline of 24 September. It is a stack-based buffer overflow in the CGI program of Zyxel GS1900-series managed switches — GS1900-8, 8HP, 10HP, 16, 24, 24E, 24EP, 24HPv2, 48 and 48HPv2 — that lets an unauthenticated attacker on the LAN execute operating-system commands through a crafted HTTP request. Zyxel patched it on 16 June in firmware 2.90(AAHH.2)C0 and per-model equivalents, and its advisory gives no CVSS score, so none is quoted here. GreyNoise’s report of the same day describes what it calls the first in-the-wild exploitation: a single actor, active since 7 May, exploited 996 GS1900 switches in 48 countries, with Italy, the United States, Taiwan, France, South Korea and the Netherlands leading, using an obfuscated Python tool to pull configurations and root-level hashed credentials over TFTP; 564 of the victims were still on factory-default credentials. The same actor stole government records through WordPress flaws and probed Gitea, UniFi, Proxmox and PAN-OS GlobalProtect. GreyNoise infers overlap with the Red Heron activity through shared infrastructure; that is an inference. No maritime victim is named. The KEV entry says LAN-based, which in practice means the management plane is reachable from wherever the switch was plugged in — a contractor’s laptop VLAN, a crew Wi-Fi segment or a flat gatehouse network. - CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog (21 Sep 2026); GreyNoise research of 21 Sep 2026; Zyxel security advisory of 16 Jun 2026 - Zyxel advisory 16 Jun 2026; GreyNoise report and KEV addition 21 Sep 2026; federal deadline 24 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] Cisco ISE carries a CVSS 10.0 authentication bypass exploited as a zero-day — and ISE is often what separates port IT from port OT
item.category: Critical Advisory — Actively exploited, CISA KEV
item.description: Cisco published advisory cisco-sa-ISE-ABP-VNSW7Tn5 on 16 September for CVE-2026-76460, an authentication bypass in Identity Services Engine and ISE-PIC scored CVSS 10.0. An unauthenticated remote attacker can reach an API endpoint with insufficient authentication and bypass the web-based management interface. Cisco states plainly that its PSIRT “is aware of active exploitation of this vulnerability.” All versions of ISE and ISE-PIC are affected; fixes are 3.1 Patch 12, 3.2 Patch 11, 3.3 Patch 12, 3.4 Patch 7 and 3.5 Patch 4. There is no workaround — the mitigation is infrastructure access control lists restricting management traffic. CISA added the CVE to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 16 September with a three-day federal remediation deadline of 19 September, which has now passed. No attribution has been published and no critical-infrastructure targeting has been claimed; Singapore’s CSA reinforced the call to patch with alert AL-2026-126 on 21 September, and ISE 3.0 is end-of-life, so those deployments need a migration rather than a patch. The maritime relevance is architectural rather than product-specific: ISE is frequently the 802.1X and network access control policy engine that decides which ports, which contractors and which vendor laptops are allowed onto terminal, gate and crane network segments, and which remote-access sessions reach the industrial DMZ. Administrative control of that policy engine is administrative control of the boundary your Cybersecurity Plan says exists. - Cisco security advisory cisco-sa-ISE-ABP-VNSW7Tn5 and the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog — version detail via BleepingComputer - Cisco advisory published 16 Sep 2026; KEV addition 16 Sep 2026, due 19 Sep 2026 (passed); CSA Singapore alert 21 Sep 2026; re-checked 22 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] Pepperl+Fuchs IO-Link masters carry 22 flaws including two CVSS 9.8 pre-auth paths to root — and the same firmware ships under Phoenix Contact and Carlo Gavazzi badges
item.category: Advisory — IO-Link master firmware, 22 CVEs, two at CVSS 9.8 (cross-sector)
item.description: CERT@VDE published VDE-2026-014 on 16 September: Pepperl+Fuchs has fixed 22 vulnerabilities in the firmware of its ICE2-8IOL and ICE3-8IOL IO-Link master modules, found by Nozomi Networks researchers. Firmware before 1.7.4 is affected and 1.7.8 is the fix. The two worst are CVE-2026-27546, an authentication bypass, and CVE-2026-27565, unauthenticated upload of a malicious IODD file that executes shell scripts, both CVSS 9.8. The remainder, CVE-2026-27547 to -27564, are command-injection, file-inclusion and authorisation flaws between 7.2 and 8.8 that lead to root-level code execution; CVE-2026-27557 (7.5) is an unauthenticated path traversal that reads the SSH server’s private keys and CVE-2026-27553 (6.5) discloses password hashes. The same firmware ships in rebadged units, so the fix applies equally to Phoenix Contact IOL MA8 PN DI8 and IOL MA8 EIP DI8 (VDE-2026-027, 20 CVEs, same fix 1.7.8) and Carlo Gavazzi YL212 and YN115 masters (VDE-2026-028). No exploitation has been reported and no CISA advisory had appeared by 22 September. Editorial assessment: IO-Link masters sit at the sensor and actuator layer of packaged automation, so on a port they are most likely inside conveyor, bulk-handling, reefer-plant and crane sub-systems delivered by an integrator rather than anything the terminal specified by part number; that is an inference from the product class, not a reported marine deployment. - CERT@VDE advisories VDE-2026-014, VDE-2026-027 and VDE-2026-028; CVE records; Nozomi Networks Labs listing - Advisories published 16 Sep 2026; no exploitation reported as of 22 Sep 2026

item.title: [Medium] CISA’s 17 September batch — seven new ICS advisories plus one update — contains nothing maritime, which is worth recording rather than padding
item.category: Advisory — CISA ICS batch, no maritime product
item.description: CISA released eight industrial control system items on Thursday 17 September: seven new advisories, ICSA-26-260-01 through -07, plus Update A to ICSA-26-211-07. The new advisories cover Bransys ELD, Mitsubishi Electric GX Works3 and Motion Control Settings, Hitachi Energy’s FACTS Control Platform, Schneider Electric Modicon M340 controllers and communication modules, Schneider Electric NetBotz 5, ABB Ability Edgenius, and Schneider Electric PowerChute Serial Shutdown. The highest score reported in the batch is CVE-2026-15688 in Mitsubishi GX Works3, an authentication algorithm weakness affecting all versions, scored CVSS 8.8 under v3.1 and 8.7 under v4.0, with CISA listing Critical Manufacturing; that advisory and Hitachi Energy’s were still missing from CISA’s machine-readable CSAF feed on 20 September, so check their advisory pages directly. The Bransys ELD advisory covers hardcoded MQTT and FTP credentials and cleartext transmission, highest score CVSS 7.5, fixed in Android 11.00.00 and iOS 1.1.54 — electronic logging devices are commercial-trucking equipment, so the Transportation Systems label on it should not be read across to vessels or terminals. The Modicon M340 advisory (-04) republishes a 2025 Schneider advisory: CVE-2025-6625, a crafted FTP command that can cause a denial of service, CVSS 7.5 under v3.1 and 8.7 under v4.0, fixed in M340 firmware SV3.70; two of the listed communication modules are affected in all versions, so read the Schneider advisory for their mitigations. NetBotz 5 (-05) carries CVE-2026-13336, an OS command injection scored 6.4 under v3.1 and 7.3 under v4.0, plus a lower-scored SQL injection, CVE-2026-13337; both are fixed in 5.6.0. ABB Ability Edgenius (-06) is exposed to CVE-2026-31431, the “Copy Fail” Linux kernel privilege escalation, CVSS 7.8, fixed in 3.2.4.1. PowerChute Serial Shutdown (-07) has CVE-2026-13348, weak limits on repeated authentication attempts, scored 5.3 under v3.1 and 6.9 under v4.0; Schneider points to version 1.6 as the fix, so confirm the build against the vendor advisory. Scores for the Hitachi Energy advisory are not quoted here. CISA reports no exploitation for anything in the batch, and none of its CVEs is in the KEV catalog. Separately, ICSA-26-211-07 covering the Mitsubishi CC-Link IE TSN communication protocol was updated on 17 September with eight newly affected products. For a marine estate the practical filter is narrow: Modicon controllers, NetBotz environmental monitoring and PowerChute UPS shutdown software do turn up in terminal plant and port facilities, so run the inventory check; nothing in this batch touches shipboard systems. - CISA ICS advisories ICSA-26-260-01 to -07 and the ICSA-26-211-07 update — scores for -01 and -04 to -07 verified against the CISA CSAF repository; -02 and -03 not yet in the CSAF feed - Advisories released 17 Sep 2026; re-checked 22 Sep 2026 (no 22 Sep batch visible at compile time); KEV status as of the 21 Sep 2026 catalog

item.title: [High] Three Linux kernel flaws entered KEV on 18 September and their 21 September deadline has passed — the kernel is in the appliances, not just the servers
item.category: Critical Advisory — Actively exploited, CISA KEV, deadlines passed
item.description: CISA added three Linux kernel vulnerabilities to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 18 September, in two alerts, with a federal remediation deadline of 21 September that has now passed: CVE-2025-39964, a race condition in the AF_ALG crypto interface; CVE-2026-53266, an out-of-bounds write in ebtables SNAT handling; and CVE-2025-39682, a flaw in kernel TLS zero-length record handling. No actor, campaign or victim has been published for any of the three, and CVSS figures differ between the sources reviewed, so none is quoted here. The KEV listing is the fact that matters: CISA has evidence of exploitation. For a maritime estate the exposure is less the Linux servers the IT team patches monthly than the Linux that nobody patches — the operating system inside VSAT terminals, bridge and engine-room gateways, terminal edge appliances, camera recorders and crane and gate controllers, where a kernel fix arrives only when the OEM ships a firmware image. ABB’s Edgenius advisory of 17 September, fixing a different kernel flaw, is the pattern in miniature. - CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog alerts of 18 Sep 2026 — confirmed through secondary trackers because cisa.gov was unreachable at compile time - Added to KEV 18 Sep 2026; federal deadline 21 Sep 2026, passed

item.title: [High] Wärtsilä FOS-Onboard’s hard-coded key flaws are re-scored to 8.3 and adjacent-network only — and the fix is now a download
item.category: Advisory — Vessel software, hard-coded cryptographic keys (Update A)
item.description: CISA updated ICSA-26-258-02 for Wärtsilä FOS-Onboard on 24 September (Update A). The original 15 September advisory covered version 5.07.0923.01, used in the maritime transportation sector, and two hard-coded cryptographic key weaknesses, both CWE-321: CVE-2026-81855, a hard-coded client authentication key in the robot testing framework, and CVE-2026-78225, a hard-coded server key in the deployer-ng Update Controller. Update A changes three things. Both CVEs are now scored CVSS v3.1 8.3 (High), down from 9.1 and 9.0 (Critical). The attack vector for both is now adjacent network rather than network (CVSS:3.1/AV:A/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H), so an attacker would need a foothold on a network segment the software is reachable from. And the fix, version 5.08.4052.01, is now published on Wärtsilä’s FOS download site. The stated impacts are unchanged: unauthorised update delivery, code execution, or extraction of credentials to impersonate a privileged client. Wärtsilä still states the flaws are not exploitable when the product is installed as recommended, and CISA reports no known public exploitation. The lower score is not a reason to defer: on a vessel where FOS-Onboard shares a segment with crew, guest or business networks, adjacent access is not a high bar. - CISA ICS advisory ICSA-26-258-02 Update A (revision 2), verified against the CISA CSAF file change in the cisagov/CSAF repository - Advisory released 15 Sep 2026; Update A 24 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] GitLab CVSS 10 path traversal is being exploited, and port, terminal and vessel teams host more of it than they think
item.category: Advisory — Actively exploited, CISA KEV
item.description: GitLab patched CVE-2026-85706 on 10 September, a path-traversal flaw in the repository commits API that it rated CVSS 10.0 and that allows an unauthenticated attacker to read arbitrary files from a GitLab server. CISA added it to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on Friday 11 September with a remediation deadline for federal agencies of Monday 14 September. watchTowr reported it was already seeing in-the-wild probes for vulnerable servers, and Hong Kong’s CERT issued its own advisory on 14 September stating the flaw is being exploited in the wild. A second flaw fixed in the same release, CVE-2026-87719, can expose sensitive information from Enterprise Edition servers. Terminal operating system integrations, crane and gate automation scripts, EDI and port-community interfaces and vessel fleet-management tooling are routinely versioned in self-hosted GitLab at port authorities, terminal operators and ship managers. Unauthenticated file reads expose the secrets that connect shore IT to crane, gate and cargo systems. - GitLab patch release advisory and CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog — reporting via Cybersecurity Dive - GitLab patch published 10 Sep 2026; KEV listing 11 Sep 2026; reporting 14 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] Rockwell extends its PLC lock-out recovery guidance to Micro820 and Micro850 — the fifth revision of a notice written because attackers were setting passwords on exposed controllers
item.category: Advisory — Vendor hardening and recovery guidance after PLC lock-outs (cross-sector)
item.description: Rockwell Automation revised security notice SD1790 to revision 5.0 on 18 September. The notice, first issued on 30 July, carries hardening guidance and instructions for restoring access to a controller when the password is unknown, and this revision extends those instructions from MicroLogix 1100 and 1400 to Micro820 and Micro850 controllers. It references the FBI public service announcement of 30 July describing attackers remotely altering the configuration of internet-exposed PLCs, changing IP addresses and setting passwords where none existed, locking operators out. There is no CVE; the guidance is to remove controllers from internet exposure, use a VPN and firewall isolation, set strong passwords, hold offline backups, disable the controller’s HTTP server and keep firmware current. Revision 5.0 adds no new incident data. Editorial assessment: Micro800-series controllers are small-site PLCs, and on a port they turn up in the plant nobody thinks of as OT — fuel and lube dispensing, stormwater and bilge pumps, gatehouse barriers, lighting masts and small reefer plants, often installed by an electrical contractor with a cellular modem for support. No marine victim is reported; the relevance is exposure pattern, not targeting. - Rockwell Automation security notice SD1790 rev 5.0, referencing the FBI public service announcement of 30 Jul 2026 - Original notice 30 Jul 2026; revision 5.0 published 18 Sep 2026

item.title: [Medium] Nozomi’s SCALANCE LPE9403 research now runs to twelve flaws — older CVEs, a patched device, and an inventory check rather than an emergency
item.category: Advisory — Vendor patch, vulnerability research
item.description: Nozomi Networks Labs published the second part of its Siemens SCALANCE LPE9403 research on 18 September, bringing the total to twelve vulnerabilities: nine in the device firmware and three in the SINEMA Remote Connect Edge Client, with CVSS scores reported in the 5.3 to 8.5 range. Nozomi demonstrated that several can be chained to obtain root-level control of the device, which would allow telemetry manipulation, alarm suppression, access to operational data, disruption of OT services and lateral movement. Two points of framing matter. First, this is not a new critical advisory: the first part of the research, published 10 September, described four PROFINET DCP memory-corruption flaws each scored CVSS 5.3 — an uninitialised value, a NULL pointer dereference and two out-of-bounds reads — and the underlying CVEs were originally disclosed in May 2025 under ICSA-25-135-18. What happened on 15 September was CISA updating that 2025 advisory to add the SINEMA Remote Connect Edge Client and the vendor fixes, not a new disclosure. Second, Siemens has already patched: affected are LPE9403 firmware below V4.0 HF0 and SINEMA Remote Connect Edge Client through V2.1, fixed in V4.0 HF0 and later. There is no evidence of exploitation in the wild. The CVE identifiers carry 2025 prefixes despite the 2026 publication, so verify them against Siemens’ own security advisory before using them in a change record. Where terminals or vessels use the LPE9403 as an edge gateway between PROFINET-connected equipment and shore-side monitoring, root on that gateway means the SCADA view of the equipment behind it can no longer be trusted. - Nozomi Networks Labs research (parts one and two) and Siemens ProductCERT — reporting via Industrial Cyber - Underlying CVEs disclosed May 2025 (ICSA-25-135-18); research published 10 and 18 Sep 2026; CISA advisory updated 15 Sep 2026

item.title: [Medium] Moxa TN-4500B rugged switches take an unauthenticated CVSS 8.8 denial of service through the web login — fix is firmware 2.1
item.category: Advisory — Rugged Ethernet switch, unauthenticated DoS (cross-sector)
item.description: Moxa published MPSA-252620 on 18 September for CVE-2026-15579 in the TN-4500B series, firmware 2.0 and earlier. It is an out-of-bounds write in the handling of the username field on the web login page: an unauthenticated attacker who can reach the management interface can crash the switch, a denial of service scored CVSS v4 8.8. Moxa fixes it in firmware 2.1. No exploitation has been reported. The TN series is Moxa’s hardened, EN 50155-class switch line built for rolling stock and vehicles, and that is where most of it sits. Editorial assessment: The same class of hardened managed switch is what integrators put on cranes, rubber-tyred gantries, straddle carriers and shipboard networks because of the vibration and temperature envelope, so the check is worth running on mobile equipment even though no marine deployment of the TN-4500B is reported; that is an inference from the product class, not a finding. - Moxa security advisory MPSA-252620 - Advisory released 18 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] September’s ICS patch wave lands on the controllers and relays behind terminal power, cranes and shore systems
item.category: Advisory — Vendor patch cycle
item.description: Schneider Electric and Siemens shipped their September fixes on 8 September, and two items reach directly into port and vessel estates. Schneider’s most severe is an authentication flaw in the Modicon M580 and M580 Safety controllers, CVE-2026-3869 at CVSS 9.2 — the M580 family runs conveyor lines, bulk handling, pump rooms and shore-power switching at terminals across the sector. Alongside it are high-severity fixes for the PowerLogic T300 RTU, formerly Easergy T300, and EcoStruxure IT Data Center Expert, plus a medium-severity SCADAPack x70 defect. Siemens issued nine advisories, seven of them on 8 September, headlined by fourteen CVEs in Reyrolle 7SR5 protection relays where a session-identifier leak allows authentication bypass. Aveva patched four flaws in the PIMBoards component of Pipeline Integrity Monitor, including a hardcoded encryption key; CISA formalised that set on 10 September as ICSA-26-253-01 — CVE-2026-81821 and CVE-2026-81822, both CVSS 8.4, alongside CVE-2026-81823 at 5.3 and CVE-2026-81824 at 4.7, fixed in Pipeline Integrity Monitor 2025 SP1 P2. None is reported as exploited. - Schneider Electric and Siemens ProductCERT September security advisories (incl. SSA-142885) and CISA ICSA-26-253-01 — round-up via SecurityWeek - Vendor advisories published 8 Sep 2026; CISA advisory ICSA-26-253-01 published 10 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] An APT cluster whose tooling overlaps Sandworm and a cluster Talos assesses as a Qilin ransomware affiliate are exploiting Cisco firewall management — the control your USCG facility plan depends on
item.category: Critical Advisory — Actively exploited, KEV-listed
item.description: Cisco and CISA confirmed on 9 September that CVE-2026-20079 in Cisco Secure Firewall Management Center is being exploited in the wild. The flaw is a critical authentication bypass caused by an improper system process created at boot; a remote, unauthenticated attacker sends crafted HTTP requests and obtains root on the underlying operating system. Cisco shipped a fix in early March and added indicators of compromise in late July, but only disclosed active exploitation on 9 September, saying it had observed attacks from August. CISA added the CVE to its KEV catalog on 9 September with a 12 September federal remediation deadline, which has now passed. Cisco Talos reports three clusters exploiting this flaw and the earlier static-credential flaw CVE-2026-20316 (CVSS 5.3, not in KEV): UAT-12197, unattributed, used CVE-2026-20079 to deploy a web shell and malicious JAR to harvest credentials; UAT-11823, an APT that used both flaws and whose tooling overlaps with Sandworm, deployed a Cyclops Blink variant; and UAT-11988, which got in through CVE-2026-20316 alone and whose tactics Talos assesses as consistent with Qilin ransomware affiliates. On 16 September Cisco shipped a separate hardening release for ASA, FTD and FMC (cisco-sa-hardening-asaftdfmc-uvpPROhN). It fixes eight internally found flaws, CVE-2026-20329 to CVE-2026-20336, with a maximum CVSS of 9.9, and accompanies the exploited FMC flaws; none of those eight is reported exploited. The FMC advisory itself moved to version 2.6 on 16 September, replacing the earlier hot fixes with security hardening releases — fixed trains 7.0.10, 7.2.12, 7.4.8, 7.6.6, 7.7.13, 10.0.2 and 10.1.0, with no workaround — and the hardening advisory was revised again on 18 September to update the ASA fixed-release table. Talos’s post, updated 21 September, still stops short of attributing UAT-11823 to Sandworm; the overlap is in tooling. Ports and terminals should read this as a boundary problem. Network segregation between administrative systems and crane, gate, reefer and bunkering networks is a load-bearing control in USCG facility security and cyber plans, and FMC is where that segregation is defined. - Cisco security advisory update and Cisco Talos research of 9 Sep 2026, plus the CISA KEV addition of 9 Sep 2026 — reported by SecurityWeek - Advisory updated and KEV listing added 9 Sep 2026; reporting 10 Sep 2026; hardening releases 16 Sep 2026; hardening advisory rev 1.1 and Talos update 18 and 21 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] CERT Polska confirms the MikroTik “MikroTrick” chain is being exploited — the router class that quietly carries port and berth connectivity
item.category: Critical Advisory — Confirmed exploited in the wild
item.description: CERT Polska issued an alert on 9 September confirming that the MikroTik RouterOS vulnerability chain known as “MikroTrick” — previously disclosed but not confirmed exploited — is now being used in real-world attacks, observed since at least 2 September. The chain pairs an SSH authentication-bypass flaw, CVE-2026-67276 at CVSS 9.2, with an SSH privilege-escalation flaw, CVE-2026-86060 also at CVSS 9.2, to take full unauthenticated administrative control of an internet-exposed RouterOS device; a third bug, CVE-2026-67277, allows memory disclosure and denial of service through the bandwidth-test service. This is a change of state, not a new vulnerability: the flaws were already known, and what is new is confirmed exploitation. CERT Polska named no victims and no sectors, noting only that MikroTik devices are widely deployed across ISPs, data centres, enterprises and critical-infrastructure networks. Nothing ties this activity to a port, terminal or vessel operator. The reason it belongs on a maritime board is deployment pattern rather than targeting: low-cost RouterOS gear is a common choice for berth and yard wireless backhaul, remote-gate and weighbridge links, CCTV and reefer-monitoring segments, crew-welfare and contractor networks, and the small port-authority sites that sit outside the main terminal firewall estate — often installed by a contractor, rarely inventoried, and frequently reachable from the internet for support. - CERT Polska alert of 9 Sep 2026 — reported by Industrial Cyber - Exploitation confirmed 9 Sep 2026; activity observed from 2 Sep 2026; CISA KEV listing 12 Sep 2026, federal deadline 13 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] Check Point confirms its CVSS 9.8 VPN flaw is being exploited, and discloses a second, separate management-server flaw hit since July. Both are now in KEV
item.category: Critical Advisory — VPN gateway and management server, actively exploited, CISA KEV
item.description: The Dutch NCSC’s 12 September warning has come true. In an advisory published on 22 September, Check Point confirmed exploitation of CVE-2026-85102 (CVSS 9.8). The flaw is improper validation of certificate data during VPN negotiation on Security Gateways and Spark firewalls, and it allows unauthenticated remote code execution. Check Point: “Starting September 12, 2026, we observed a wave of exploitation attempts against Spark customers.” Fixes were released on 9 September. Check Point gives no customer count and no attribution. The indicators it published are exploitation certificates with subjects CN=vpn, CN=vpn-user or CN=vpnuser, OU=users, O=global. CISA added CVE-2026-85102 to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 22 September, with a federal deadline of 25 September. Its companion CVE-2026-85103, named in the NCSC warning, was not among that day’s KEV additions. The same advisory discloses a different flaw, CVE-2026-93616 (CVSS 9.8). It is a pre-authentication path traversal in the Security Management web service that leads to script execution. Check Point reports a handful of pinpointed attacks on 23 July, so it was a zero-day for about two months; a fix became available on 22 September and it also entered KEV that day. The maritime relevance is the same as before, now with confirmed activity behind it. Ashore, these gateways terminate the terminal operating system’s links to customs, shipping lines and haulier portals, and the vendor tunnels into crane, gate and reefer systems. Spark appliances are the small-office firewall class that agency, forwarder and vessel-management offices tend to run. Afloat, VPN concentrators in front of satellite links are how OEMs reach propulsion, power-management and navigation equipment for remote diagnostics. - Check Point security advisory (22 Sep 2026); CISA KEV alert of 22 Sep 2026; earlier Dutch National Cyber Security Centre warning reported by BleepingComputer. No maritime victims named - Gateway fixes 9 Sep 2026; NCSC warning 12 Sep 2026; exploitation observed from 12 Sep 2026; advisory, management-server fix and KEV additions 22 Sep 2026; federal deadline 25 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] Arista’s on-premises VeloCloud Orchestrator carries an exploited CVSS 10 flaw, and the orchestrator is what configures every SD-WAN edge at your terminals and offices
item.category: Critical Advisory — SD-WAN orchestrator, actively exploited, CISA KEV
item.description: Arista published Security Advisory 0183 on 22 September for CVE-2026-93952, an improper input validation flaw (CWE-20) in on-premises VeloCloud Orchestrator (VCO), scored CVSS 3.1 10.0. Without authentication or user interaction, a remote attacker can reach privileged internal functionality and affect the VCO host. Arista says the flaw is being actively exploited in the wild. The flaw applies only where certificate-based authentication from VeloCloud Edge to VCO is configured, and the attacker needs the public portion of an Edge certificate. Affected trains are 5.2.3.15 and earlier, 6.1.3.7 and earlier, 6.4.2.7 and earlier, and 7.0.0.2 and earlier. Fixed releases are 5.2.3.16+ and 6.4.2.8+; the advisory lists no fix yet for the 6.1.x or 7.0.x trains. Hosted VCO has already been patched. CISA added the CVE to KEV on 22 September with a federal deadline of 25 September. Arista’s indicators include the HTTP header x-vc-opt and connections from 142.93.149.77 and 104.248.126.159. No victims or attribution have been published. Editorial assessment: SD-WAN is a common way to link port offices, inland depots, remote terminals and vessel-management sites. The orchestrator pushes configuration and routing to every edge, so a compromise here can reshape the paths into OT-adjacent segments at every connected site at once. - Arista Security Advisory 0183; CISA KEV alert of 22 Sep 2026. Maritime relevance is an editorial assessment; no maritime victim has been named - Advisory published 22 Sep 2026; added to KEV 22 Sep 2026; federal deadline 25 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] CISA adds five exploited flaws to KEV, including the remote-support tool crane and TOS vendors log in with
item.category: Critical Advisory — Confirmed exploited, remote-support tooling
item.description: CISA added five vulnerabilities affecting JFrog Artifactory, ConnectWise ScreenConnect and MikroTik RouterOS to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 10 and 11 September after evidence of active exploitation, with federal remediation deadlines of 13 September for RouterOS, 14 September for ScreenConnect and 25 September for Artifactory. Reporting indicates the Artifactory flaws were chained to gain administrator control, establish persistence and install Rust-based backdoors, while ScreenConnect exploitation reportedly enabled unauthorised file transfer and execution through active sessions using a malicious VBScript payload. The RouterOS entry is the CERT Polska chain carried separately here. For a terminal or port authority the ScreenConnect item is the one worth acting on: remote-support agents are how crane, gate, weighbridge, reefer-monitoring and terminal-operating-system vendors reach equipment out on the quay, and they are usually installed at commissioning by a contractor and never revisited. - CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog addition — reported by The Hacker News - KEV additions 10 Sep (RouterOS) and 11 Sep 2026 (ScreenConnect, Artifactory); reporting 13 Sep 2026; federal deadlines 13, 14 and 25 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] CISA refreshed the iDirect VSAT advisory on 10 September — the flaws are July’s, and the terminals are still on the vessel
item.category: Advisory — Shipboard VSAT terminal, advisory updated in-window
item.description: Be precise about what moved this week. CISA advisory ICSA-26-183-01 was originally published on 2 July 2026 and was updated on 10 September; nothing new was discovered, and the update is the reason it appears here rather than any fresh finding. It covers ST Engineering iDirect Evolution iQ Series, 3315 Series and 9 Series satellite terminals up to firmware 4.5.2.1. CVE-2026-38059 is a missing-authentication flaw that exposes the terminal’s REST interface, including an identity endpoint, without a login — serial numbers, device identifiers and terminal private keys can be read by anyone who can reach it, rated CVSS 7.5 under v3 and 8.7 under v4. CVE-2026-38057 is a cross-site request forgery against the reboot endpoint allowing a remote denial of service, rated CVSS 8.1 under v3 and 7.0 under v4. The fix is firmware 4.5.2.2 or later, and no exploitation has been confirmed. What makes this a fleet problem rather than a patch item is the position of the device. The VSAT terminal is usually the vessel’s only link, and the same path carries chart and route updates, engine and cargo telemetry, safety-management traffic, crew welfare and, in most modern arrangements, the shoreside remote support OEMs use to reach machinery systems. A reboot loop takes all of that at once, at sea, with no local engineer. And a leaked terminal private key is a different kind of loss again — it is a credential, so installing firmware does not retire it. - CISA ICS advisory ICSA-26-183-01, republishing ST Engineering iDirect guidance — advisory update noted in OT security reporting of 11 Sep 2026 - Originally disclosed 2 Jul 2026; CISA advisory updated 10 Sep 2026 — the update introduced no new vulnerability

item.title: [Info] CISA and FBI warn that an integrator’s network is part of your attack surface — and the case they cite involved transportation customers
item.category: Guidance — CISA and FBI joint fact sheet on third-party ICS integrator risk; transportation named among the compromised provider’s customers; no CVE
item.description: CISA and the FBI published a joint fact sheet on 24 September, “Considerations for Critical Infrastructure Operators Working with Third-Party ICS Integrators”. The case it cites: foreign cyber actors accessed a US industrial automation solutions provider between March and April 2025 and created nine .zip archives of roughly 800 files for presumed exfiltration, including customer SCADA information, ICS device details and other schematics. The provider’s customers included power utilities and transportation entities. The fact sheet does not name the provider, its customers or the actor, does not say whether any customer was maritime, and describes no disruption. Its recommendations: give integrators only the minimum access a task requires, make them connect through routes the operator can monitor, write cybersecurity and supply-chain requirements — data storage, remote access, patch management — into contracts and service agreements, and establish what data each integrator can reach and where it is stored. For ports and fleets the integrator population is large: crane and automation OEMs, terminal operating system and gate vendors, engine and cargo-system service providers, and the contractors who install CCTV, reefer monitoring and yard wireless. This is guidance prompted by a prior case, not a new incident. - CISA and FBI joint fact sheet; WaterISAC TLP:CLEAR re-post; reported by Industrial Cyber and SecurityWeek - Published 24 Sep 2026

item.title: [Medium] NIST’s draft SP 800-82 Rev. 4 brings maritime vessels into scope for the first time, and comments close on 30 November
item.category: Guidance — NIST OT security standard, draft for comment
item.description: NIST released the initial public draft of SP 800-82 Revision 4, its guide to operational technology security, on 22 September. The 321-page draft is open for public comment until 30 November 2026. The scope expands to cover maritime vessels alongside building automation, water and wastewater, food and agriculture, freight rail and industrial IoT. The draft builds in CSF 2.0 and zero trust, and it is explicit about the mindset: “A mature OT defense mindset is consequence-driven. Cyber controls should be evaluated alongside engineering countermeasures that can remove or reduce the impact of a successful attack.” It calls privileged access management the clearest expression of zero trust in OT, because each privileged session is evaluated and authorised individually. It also says segmentation should extend within OT, separating process-control traffic from the management networks that carry configuration, patching and access. This is draft guidance with no mandatory force, but 800-82 is the reference that auditors, class societies and US regulators tend to cite. Naming vessels in scope gives shipboard OT a NIST baseline it has not had before. - NIST SP 800-82 Rev. 4 initial public draft — reporting and quotations via Industrial Cyber - Draft released 22 Sep 2026; comments due 30 Nov 2026

item.title: [Info] CISA’s Cyber Storm X put a nation-state adversary against ports, rail and water. The public after-action report is the part to watch for
item.category: Guidance — CISA national exercise, transportation and water
item.description: CISA ran Cyber Storm X, its national cybersecurity exercise, as reported by Industrial Cyber on 22 September. The four-day event had about 2,000 participants from more than 200 organisations across the public and private sectors and all levels of government. The scenario was a nation-state adversary targeting transportation systems, including rail and ports, and the water and wastewater sector. The stated aim was to test the policies, processes and procedures used to identify and respond to significant multi-sector cyber incidents affecting critical infrastructure. “Cyber Storm helps critical infrastructure owners and operators understand how we would manage a large-scale cyber incident,” said Acting CISA Director Nick Andersen. CISA says it will compile lessons learned into a public after-action report with observations, analyses and recommendations. The exact exercise dates were not published in the coverage. This is an exercise, not an incident, and no real-world activity is implied. - CISA announcement of Cyber Storm X — reporting and Nick Andersen quotation via Industrial Cyber - Reported 22 Sep 2026; exercise dates not published; after-action report pending

item.title: [Info] CISA’s cyber decoys guide is aimed squarely at networks you are not allowed to change
item.category: Guidance — CISA detection and response
item.description: CISA published “Using Cyber Decoys to Strengthen Detection and Response” on 17 September, a guide for critical infrastructure owners on deploying decoys, honeytokens and tripwires. It defines decoys as assets that appear to be legitimate systems, accounts or data but exist to distract adversaries, detect their presence and support threat-intelligence collection, and it structures the work in three phases — preparation, execution and analysis — positioned alongside zero trust rather than as a replacement for it. The reason it matters for maritime is the constraint it works within. Terminal and shipboard networks are the environments where agents cannot be installed, protocols cannot be probed and a scanner is a genuine operational risk, which is why detection coverage there tends to lag the corporate estate by years. A decoy adds nothing to a production controller and touches no cargo or navigation process, but it produces a high-confidence alert the moment someone is enumerating a network they should not be on. This is guidance, not an advisory: there is no CVE, no product and no exploitation associated with it. - CISA guide “Using Cyber Decoys to Strengthen Detection and Response” — reporting via SecurityWeek and Industrial Cyber - Published 17 Sep 2026

item.title: [Info] ENISA switches on the Single Reporting Platform as the Cyber Resilience Act’s vulnerability reporting duties take effect
item.category: Regulation & Policy — EU Cyber Resilience Act
item.description: The EU Agency for Cybersecurity deployed the initial operating capability of its Single Reporting Platform, announced 14 September, giving manufacturers and open-source software stewards the channel they need to meet Cyber Resilience Act reporting obligations that took effect this month. Under the CRA, makers of products with digital elements must report actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents on a defined clock, with an early warning followed by a fuller notification. Shipowners, ports and terminals are not the regulated party, but the vendors of navigation, cargo, crane and bridge equipment sold into the EU are, and IACS UR E26/E27 evidence expectations sit alongside this neatly. Reported here factually as a regulatory milestone, without comment on the underlying policy debate. - ENISA announcement of the Single Reporting Platform initial operating capability — reporting via Industrial Cyber - Announced and reported 14 Sep 2026; CRA reporting obligations effective September 2026

item.title: [Info] EU Cyber Resilience Act reporting went live on 11 September — bridge and engine-room equipment makers now have 24 hours
item.category: Regulation & Policy — EU, now in force
item.description: The vulnerability and incident reporting obligations of the EU Cyber Resilience Act took effect on 11 September 2026. Manufacturers of products with digital elements must now notify an actively exploited vulnerability or a severe security incident through ENISA’s Single Reporting Platform within 24 hours of becoming aware, follow up within 72 hours with exploit and mitigation detail, and file a final report within 14 days of a fix being available, as well as informing affected users. The regime applies to manufacturers placing products on the EU market wherever they are based, with penalties up to €15 million. For shipowners, managers and terminals this sits alongside rather than inside the IMO, IACS and USCG framework: it does not change what you must report, but it changes what your suppliers must tell you and when. Navigation, propulsion-control, power-management, AIS, ECDIS and terminal-automation vendors selling into Europe are now on a 24-hour clock. - European Commission CRA reporting guidance and ENISA Single Reporting Platform — reported by Dark Reading - Obligations in force from 11 Sep 2026

item.title: [Info] 117 federal incident-reporting rules across 27 agencies — and a maritime operator can be inside several of them at once
item.category: Regulation & Policy — Incident reporting burden
item.description: The McCrary Institute and the US Chamber of Commerce published analysis on 8 September, drawing on GAO work, counting 117 federal cyber incident reporting regulations spread across 27 agencies, 48 of which apply to private industry. Their argument is operational rather than political: duplicative filings with different thresholds, formats and clocks pull the same handful of people off containment during the first hours of an incident. Maritime is a clear example of the overlap. A single event at a US-flagged vessel or an MTSA-regulated facility can trigger reporting to the National Response Center under 33 CFR 101 Subpart F, a Coast Guard Captain of the Port notification, and, once CIRCIA rules are finalised — expected this autumn — a separate CISA filing, on top of any flag-state, class or charterer obligation. - McCrary Institute and US Chamber of Commerce analysis citing GAO findings — via Industrial Cyber - Published 8 Sep 2026; CIRCIA final rule expected autumn 2026

item.title: [Medium] The Coast Guard now has one office that owns maritime cyber policy — expect the inspections to sharpen
item.category: Regulation — US Coast Guard maritime cyber governance
item.description: The US Coast Guard has stood up the Office of Maritime Cybersecurity Policy (CG-MCP) as the central authority for cybersecurity policy covering ports, vessels and facilities across the Marine Transportation System, reporting to the Director of Inspections and Compliance. Its remit is to write policy, run a unified compliance strategy, coordinate enforcement and industry engagement, and track emerging technology and cyber risk. The move follows Government Accountability Office findings about gaps in Coast Guard cyber oversight. Nothing in the MTS cyber rule changes today, but the practical effect of consolidating policy and compliance under one office is usually consistency: the same questions, asked the same way, at more facilities. - US Coast Guard ALCOAST 266/26 and Coast Guard news release — corroborated by ExecutiveGov and Industrial Cyber - Office establishment announced Aug 2026; reported 1 Sep 2026
